text: Chapter six. Gold: is there money without a cave?
Every money in this episode had a Wren. A ship on Yap. Glass from Venice. Iron drills. Shells from Zanzibar. A mint in Rome. Each time, money got easier to make. Usually, the savers paid.
Now gold. All the gold ever mined would fit in one cube, about twenty-three metres on each side. As tall as a seven-storey building. Almost all of it still exists.
Each year, the world's mines add a slice on top, less than half a metre thick. Under two percent.

Gold had its rushes. California in eighteen forty-nine, then Australia. In the eighteen-fifties, the world dug over three times as much gold a year as in the forties. Three times a thin slice is still a thin slice.
Prices rose. In Britain, where money was gold, by up to a third. They stayed high for about twenty years. Then they fell. By the eighteen-nineties, they were lower than in the forties.

Compare. Cowries: a silver dollar cost ten times more shells. Rome: wheat cost thirty-seven times more. Gold, in the great rushes: prices up to a third higher, for a while. Gold came closest to money without a cave.
And today? In ten years, gold's price roughly tripled, with big swings. So digging it pays far more. Still, mine output grew under one percent a year. Nobody has found gold's cave.
Our money today isn't gold. So who is its Wren? First: why is gold so hard to flood? Next episode: why gold.
